title: Investor Types and Their Liabilities
notes:
THE ARGUMENT OF THE SLIDE

Every investor starts from what it owes, not from the asset. A pension fund owes benefits that run for decades and are often linked to inflation, and the OECD's survey paper says exactly why that makes infrastructure attractive to it: such investments can assist liability-driven investment and duration hedging, projects are long-term investments that could match the long duration of pension liabilities, and inflation-linked assets could hedge the sensitivity of liabilities to rising inflation (Della Croce 2012, Executive summary, page 7). The same paper adds that listed infrastructure moves with broader markets, so unlisted infrastructure is held for diversification although it is illiquid (page 7). The other rows describe how the rest of the investor universe differs from the pension fund, and they are my summary of the standard account, not a finding I have checked paper by paper.

WHAT IS VERIFIED AND WHAT IS NOT

Verified in the sources I read: the pension-fund row (OECD, page 7); that insurers and banks appear as investors in closed funds and direct deals, that sovereign wealth funds and government agencies (including development banks such as the IFC, the EIB and CDC Group) invest directly far more than through funds, and that endowments and foundations use closed funds almost exclusively (Andonov, Kräussl and Rauh 2021, Figure 1, page 3888; see slide 5); and that regulators have begun to treat infrastructure differently from private equity: a 2017 amendment to the Solvency II Delegated Regulation reduced the capital insurers must hold against the equity of qualifying infrastructure projects (Andonov et al., introduction; I did not read the regulation). Not verified here: the constraints in the last column for insurers, sovereign wealth funds, endowments and development institutions. They come from the earlier Week 3 deck (slides 6, 9 and 11 of the old 82-slide deck), which cites Abor and others (2025) chapters 14 to 16 and Gatti chapter 8, neither of which I re-read. The old deck itself says the capital-regime detail should be confirmed before delivery.

TEACHING POINT

Ask which of these investors can hold a forty-year asset for forty years. Sovereign funds, a few very large pension plans and strategic corporates can. Everyone else is a temporary owner, and a fund with a ten-year life makes that explicit (slide 8). The last column anticipates the week's next sections: governance capacity and scale decide the route the investor takes (slide 5).

RETURN TO THIS IN THE CASE

The case investor is a pension scheme. This slide supplies the vocabulary for asking why a scheme invests in a fund at all, and what it needs from the asset before it commits.

title: Allocations Differ Widely across Pension Funds
notes:
THE FIGURE

Della Croce (2012), Table 5 on printed page 23: infrastructure investment as a percentage of total assets in 2010 for the 14 large pension funds with a separate infrastructure allocation. Unlisted equity (green), listed equity (ochre) and fixed income (blue). OMERS 15.5, AustralianSuper 11.8, Superannuation NZ 9.9, OTPP 9.3, CPPIB 6.8, Sunsuper 4.5, UniSuper 4.4, Future Fund 4.1, USS 2.9, PFZW 2.0, PFA 0.7, PMT 0.6, GEPF 0.3 and ABP 0.3. The unlisted-equity dollar figures in the table sum to USD 37,629 million against the printed total of 37,630 (rounding).

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

The survey covered 52 institutional investors with USD 7.7 trillion of assets, of which 28 funds with USD 1.4 trillion of assets invested in infrastructure and are used here (pages 4 and 8). Their infrastructure investment at the end of 2010 was USD 41.8 billion, 2.9 per cent of those funds' assets and 0.5 per cent of the whole survey. Of it, USD 37.9 billion (2.6 per cent) was unlisted equity, split USD 30.9 billion direct and USD 7.0 billion through funds, and USD 3.9 billion (0.3 per cent) was fixed income (page 8). The averages hide the spread, which runs from 15.5 per cent at OMERS, with a stated target of 21.5 per cent, to 0.3 per cent at ABP (pages 8 and 23).

CAUTIONS

The data are for 2010 and are the oldest figures in the deck; the OECD's later surveys would be better and I could not retrieve them. The sample is of large funds and is biased towards the larger investors in each country (page 4). Listed infrastructure holdings are mostly buried in the equity allocation, so totals are understated (note to Table 5, page 23). The paper's reasons for small allocations include the cost of building expertise and the form of access; the old Week 3 deck (slide 10) adds consultant and peer anchoring, which I did not verify here.

RETURN TO THIS IN THE CASE

The spread is why a scheme's own history matters. A fund with a 15 per cent allocation has built a team and a track record, and one with 0.3 per cent has not, which bears on what a smaller scheme asks of a manager.

title: Routes Used by Institutional Investors
notes:
THE FIGURE

Andonov, Kräussl and Rauh (2021), Figure 1 (printed page 3888): the observations in their data by investor type and by route into infrastructure. Closed funds account for 538 funds, 5,189 investor-fund observations and 59,779 investor-deal observations. Direct investments account for 2,049 investor-deal observations. Listed funds account for 271 investor-fund observations and open-ended funds for 460. By investor type, closed funds: public pension funds 1,831, private pension funds 1,386, government agencies 438, insurance firms and banks 944, sovereign wealth funds 98, endowments and foundations 492 (these sum to 5,189). Direct investments: 831, 162, 479, 276, 294 and 7 (sum 2,049).

The chart plots, for each investor type, closed-fund observations as a share of closed-fund plus direct observations: endowments 99 per cent, private pension funds 90, insurers and banks 77, public pension funds 69, government agencies 48, sovereign wealth funds 25. The shares are my arithmetic. They mix two units, because closed-fund observations count investor-fund pairs and direct observations count investor-deal pairs, so they show the relative use of each route and not dollars. The authors report that dollar commitments to closed funds are an order of magnitude larger than to open-ended funds (footnote 6, page 3888) and that closed funds represent the lion's share of commitments and the majority of the dollar value of deals (page 3882).

THE POINTS

The second structure in importance is the direct deal. Direct deals are implemented by a small number of deep-pocketed investors and are not applicable to most institutions, because they need very large commitments to one asset and specialised staff (page 3882). Footnote 2 on that page gives the concentration: the top 20 investors account for 55 per cent of investor-deal observations in direct deals but under 10 per cent of investor-fund observations in closed funds. US institutions made 2,330 commitments to closed funds but only 62 direct investments. The table of investors on slide 3 predicts this ordering, with sovereign funds and government agencies most direct and endowments and private pension funds most dependent on funds.

WHY THIS BEGINS THE FUND PART

The route is the reason a limited partner meets the fund contract. The next section takes the closed fund as the vehicle, because it is the route most investors use.

RETURN TO THIS IN THE CASE

A local pension scheme is an investor without the scale to invest directly. The case shows what it does instead.

title: Funding the Data Centre
notes:
THE FIGURE

Van Nieuwerburgh (2026), Financing the AI buildout, NBER Working Paper 35865 (October 2026; the version forthcoming in the Brookings Papers on Economic Activity, Fall 2026). Figure 1 (printed page 7): capital expenditure and operating cash flow of Oracle, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta and Alphabet, US$ billion. Capex: 96.8 (2020), 130.9, 158.3, 153.8, 240.4, 415.8 (2025) and 800.5 (2026, projected). Operating cash flow: 252.2, 289.9, 288.3, 377.9, 478.5, 603.2 and 707.1. I read these from the data labels on the figure, and the text confirms the endpoints on page 2 (about $97 billion in 2020, more than $400 billion in 2025, projected above $800 billion in 2026, and capex surpassing combined operating cash flow for the first time in 2026). The percentage under each year is capex over operating cash flow, my arithmetic: 38, 45, 55, 41, 50, 69 and 113. The 2026 values combine reported results with company guidance and Wall Street estimates, and the figure excludes capex for data centres the hyperscalers lease, so it understates the investment of the system as a whole (notes to Figure 1).

THE SCALE

The paper estimates a 1 GW AI campus costs about $41 billion, about $41 million per MW, of which about $11 million is the real estate asset (including cooling and backup power), $2 million the power infrastructure and $28 million the GPU racks, network and storage (page 4). A 188 GW completed buildout over 2025 to 2032 would need nearly $9 trillion, $8.973 trillion in the paper's central scenario, which is 3.22 per cent of GDP a year, more than the canal, railroad, electrification, highway and telecom booms (Table 1, page 5; the paper calls it a scenario and not a forecast, and its cancellation rates are set out on page 4).

THE FINANCING POINT

Internal cash flow no longer covers capex, so hyperscalers combine direct ownership with leases, joint ventures, project finance, private credit and structured finance (pages 2 and 6). Morgan Stanley is quoted as estimating that more than half of about $2.9 trillion needed for hyperscalers' incremental compute over 2025 to 2028 will come from outside capital, with roughly a 60 to 40 equity to debt split and, within debt, about $800 billion of private credit, $200 billion of corporate debt and $150 billion of structured finance (page 8). That is a secondary citation and should be treated as an estimate by one bank.

HOW IT LINKS TO THE FUND MODELS

The outside equity is mostly infrastructure funds, real estate investment trusts, developers and private equity (page 2), which are the vehicles of the next section. A data centre fund has the capital calls and distributions of the first model, the fee and carry terms of the second, and an obsolescence problem that the first model cannot see, because GPUs have economic lives much shorter than the debt that finances them (page 7). The third model asks whether a long-lived, contracted asset hedges a long-lived liability; the paper's evidence that data centre REIT betas have risen from about 0.5 to about 1 (page 13) bears on the correlation assumptions in that model.

RETURN TO THIS IN THE CASE

Lightly. The case investor sits among the investors who supply equity to vehicles like these, and the question of what a limited partner needs to know about the asset's life before it commits is the same.

This slide covers private capital and vehicles, the Week 3 aspect of the course's data-centre thread. Scale and booms, local incidence and the grid, and the environmental and social aspects belong to other weeks.

title: The Capital Stack of a Data Centre
notes:
THE TABLE

A general account of who supplies each layer of a data centre financing, from Van Nieuwerburgh (2026), pages 2 and 6 to 10. The tenant is an investment-grade hyperscaler (Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, Alphabet and Oracle are investment-grade borrowers; frontier AI firms such as OpenAI and Anthropic generally lack standalone credit profiles and reach compute through contracts with hyperscalers, page 6). Data centre developers, infrastructure funds, REITs and private equity provide equity, and banks, private credit funds and securitisation vehicles supply debt (page 2). Bank loans include mortgage loans backed by data centre assets and syndicated lines of credit, and private credit and structured finance provide a growing share of project funding, usually backed by long-term contracted revenues (page 7). GPUs and related hardware can be financed by leases or asset-backed structures, though the collateral has a shorter economic life and obsolescence risk (page 7). The aggregate 60 to 40 equity to debt split can understate leverage at the asset level, because shells and power infrastructure are financed through project-level debt, leases and other asset-backed structures while hyperscalers spend internal capital on IT equipment (page 8).

THE HYPERION ILLUSTRATION (CHECK EACH FIGURE)

Meta's Hyperion data centre in Louisiana, a project of about 2.0 GW and about $30 billion, about $15 million per MW excluding IT equipment (page 8 and footnote 3). Meta initially owned it, then sold an 80 per cent equity stake to Blue Owl for approximately $2.5 billion; the joint venture, Beignet, raised $27 billion of external debt in October 2025, rated A+ by Standard and Poor's, one notch below Meta's own corporate rating, described as the largest individual investment-grade corporate debt issuance in US history (page 8). Debt is roughly $27 billion of the $30 billion asset value, a debt-to-asset ratio of about 90 per cent, and the debt service coverage ratio is 1.12 times (page 9). The debt carries a yield of 6.58 per cent, at least 100 basis points above what Meta would likely have paid on comparable unsecured debt, which the paper says implies more than $5 billion of additional interest over the life of the financing (page 10). Meta leases the campus in five four-year leases from 2029 to the bond's 2049 maturity; at each renewal it may terminate for some or all of the campus, and must cover any shortfall between sale proceeds and a contractually specified minimum value, a residual value guarantee (page 9). Meta does not recognise the future lease obligations or the guarantee on its balance sheet until they take effect (page 9). The structure is a network of bankruptcy-remote special-purpose vehicles (Figure 2, page 10).

I checked each of these figures against the October NBER text and they agree with it. Please check them against S&P's pre-sale report, which the paper cites for Figure 2, before anything is quoted in a published case. The earlier September Brookings conference draft differed, which is why the NBER version is used here. The figure of $2.5 billion for the 80 per cent stake and the characterisation as the largest investment-grade corporate issuance are the paper's, and I have not verified either independently.

RISK AND RETURN POINT

The paper's Figure 3 shows the market beta of publicly traded data centre REITs rising from about 0.5 to around 1 (page 13), so data centres look less like defensive infrastructure and more like part of the same systematic risk complex. That is the Andonov et al. conclusion for closed funds (slide 16), reached from a different asset.

HOW IT LINKS TO THE FUND MODELS

The residual value guarantee is a put option written by the tenant to the lender, which is the same family of claim as the carry in the second model. A five-year, four-year-lease structure on a 20-year bond means the asset must be re-let or sold at each renewal, which is the timing question of the first model. The bond investors who need long, predictable cash flows are the liability-matching investors of the third model.

RETURN TO THIS IN THE CASE

Lightly. Both the case and this table are about who holds the equity claim in a vehicle and on what terms.

title: The Fund as the Vehicle
notes:
THE FOCUS OF THE WEEK

Helen's brief for the deck was that there is never enough time to elaborate each topic and the week should choose. The choice here is the closed-end fund, because it is the vehicle most investors use (slide 5), because a single fund brings together three questions that any investor must answer, and because the evidence in the next part is about funds. The three questions each have a model and an interactive page, and the section is meant to be general. It is a general account of the fund and the investor's problem, and not a preview of any one transaction.

THE STRUCTURE

A closed infrastructure fund is raised for a specified period, typically 10 to 12 years with possible short extensions, and is governed by a partnership agreement between the investors, who act as limited partners and commit capital at the start (the vintage year), and the general partner who manages it (Andonov, Kräussl and Rauh 2021, page 3888). Metrick and Yasuda say limited partnerships typically last 10 years and that the payments to the general partner have fixed and variable components defined in the agreement at inception (2007 working paper, page 2). The fund calls capital over several years, invests it, and returns it as assets are sold.

THE THREE QUESTIONS

When does the money move? The Takahashi and Alexander cash-flow model (slides 9 and 10). Who is paid for what? The Metrick and Yasuda treatment of fees and carried interest as claims (slides 11 and 12). What does the investor need the asset to do? The Keel and Müller surplus model, after Sharpe and Tint (slides 13 and 14). Slide 15 compares them. Each page opens on a generic setting and offers the announced terms of one real fund as one starting point among others, together with a starting point from the academic evidence.

WHY THREE AND NOT MORE

They are three distinct parts of the investor's problem and none can be derived from another. The deck does not cover listed infrastructure, open-ended funds, co-investment, the secondary market or fund-of-funds structures; the earlier 82-slide deck has them at slides 14 to 19.

SOURCES

Andonov, Kräussl and Rauh (2021), page 3888; Metrick and Yasuda, The economics of private equity funds, Wharton Rodney L. White Center Working Paper 17-07 (September 2007), page 2 (printed page equals PDF page minus 1); the published version is Review of Financial Studies 23(6), 2010, 2303 to 2341, which I did not retrieve.

RETURN TO THIS IN THE CASE

All three questions return in the case: the structure and terms of the fund, the investor's reasons for committing, and the return, risk and exit. The questions in the case echo these slides.

title: Takahashi and Alexander (2002): Cash Flows
notes:
THE MODEL

Takahashi, D. and Alexander, S. (2002), Illiquid alternative asset fund modeling, Journal of Portfolio Management 28(2), 90 to 100. I could not retrieve the original article. The three equations and the six inputs are taken from the description in Karatas, Klinkert and Hirsa (2021), Supervised neural networks for illiquid alternative asset cash flow forecasting, arXiv 2108.02853, page 3, which uses the Yale model as its benchmark, and from Luxenberg and co-authors (2022), Strategic asset allocation with illiquid alternatives, arXiv 2207.07767, pages 5 and 9. They describe a discrete-time deterministic model with six inputs: the rate of contribution RC, the capital commitment CC, the life of the fund L, the bow factor B describing how the rate of distribution changes over time, the annual growth rate G, and the yield Y. The three equations are C(t) = RC(t) x (CC minus paid-in capital to t-1); D(t) = RD(t) x NAV(t-1) x (1+G), where RD(t) = max[Y, (t/L) to the power B]; and NAV(t) = NAV(t-1) x (1+G) + C(t) minus D(t). Calls are a fraction of uncalled commitment, distributions a fraction of asset value, and growth is constant.

THE LIMITS

The authors of both descriptions note the drawbacks. The model is deterministic, its inputs are set by the investor's judgement (the rate of contribution, bow factor and life) while growth is projected from data, and calls and distributions depend on one another so calibration to recent data is hard (Karatas et al., page 3). Luxenberg et al. replace it with a stochastic model whose intensities are random (page 9). Furenstam and Forsell (2018), cited by Karatas et al., compared the model with a stochastic alternative on empirical data; I did not read that thesis.

TWO SIMPLIFICATIONS OF MINE

Calls stop after an investment period, and the value left in the final year is paid out in full, so the J-curve closes and the fund ends with no residual. The original lets calls continue geometrically and leaves a residual value. In the page the net internal rate of return equals the growth rate G, because every pound compounds at G, so the page teaches the timing and liquidity of the commitment and not the return.

WHY IT MATTERS FOR AN INVESTOR

A commitment is not an exposure. An investor that wants an exposure of a given size must commit more than that size and then wait for it to build, and it must hold cash for calls that arrive before distributions do. The model is the standard tool for that planning, and Luxenberg et al. build strategic allocation on it.

RETURN TO THIS IN THE CASE

The case section on the structure and terms of the fund and the question of when a pension scheme's cash goes out and comes back.

SOURCES

Karatas, T., Klinkert, F. and Hirsa, A. (2021), arXiv 2108.02853, pages 3 to 4; Luxenberg, E., Boyd, S., Kochenderfer, M. and co-authors (2022), arXiv 2207.07767, pages 5 and 9; Takahashi and Alexander (2002) as cited (not retrieved).

title: The J-Curve of a Ten-Year Fund
notes:
INTERACTIVE: web/fund-cash-flows.html (button at top right)

THE FIGURE

The generic setting of the page: a commitment of 100 to a closed-end fund with a ten-year life, rates of contribution of 25, 33, 50 and 50 per cent of the uncalled commitment in years 1 to 4 (and 50 per cent afterwards until calls stop in year 5), a bow factor of 2.5, a minimum yield of 3 per cent and net growth of 9 per cent. The bars are the net cash flow in each year (green when positive); the line is the cumulative net cash flow, the J-curve. The investor's deepest cumulative outlay is about 75 per 100 committed, in year 4, and the cumulative net flow turns positive in year 8. Distributions total about 136 on calls of about 94 (not all the commitment is called, because calls stop after year 5 and each year takes only a share of what remains), a multiple of 1.45, and the cumulative net flow ends at about 42. All inputs other than the 9 per cent growth are illustrative.

WHAT THE PAGE ADDS

title: Metrick and Yasuda (2010): Fees as Claims
notes:
THE PAPER

Metrick, A. and Yasuda, A. (2010), The economics of private equity funds, Review of Financial Studies 23(6), 2303 to 2341. I read the Wharton Rodney L. White Center working paper 17-07 of 15 September 2007, whose printed page is the PDF page minus one; the published version was not retrieved, and the two differ in sample and some figures (the working paper reports 238 funds raised from 1992 to 2006, 94 venture capital and 144 buyout, and about 60 per cent of expected revenue as fixed; I have not compared it with the published figures).

THE IDEA

Fund managers earn revenue from fees and profit-sharing rules. The authors build a model of expected revenue as a function of those rules (abstract, page 1). Virtually all private equity funds are limited partnerships with the firm as general partner and large institutions as limited partners, lasting about 10 years, and the partnership agreement sets the payments, which have a fixed component, like the pricing terms of mutual funds, and a variable component, which has no analogue among most mutual funds (pages 2 and 3). Four concepts define carried interest: the carry level, the basis, the hurdle and the timing (page 11), and a catch-up lets the manager recover what the hurdle withheld (page 12). The key step is to value carried interest as 'like a fractional call option on the total proceeds of all investments, with this fraction equal to the carry level and the strike price of the call equal to the carry basis' (Section III.B, page 16). Their model simulates the exit dates and returns of each investment and solves for the value at which limited partners earn their cost of capital after the manager is paid (pages 16 and 23).

THE RESULT

About 60 per cent of expected revenue comes from fixed components that do not depend on performance (abstract). For a venture capital fund the present value of carry per $100 committed is $8.63 in the base case (20 per cent carry on committed capital, no hurdle, 25 investments) and $8.29 with an 8 per cent hurdle and catch-up; for a buyout fund it is $5.88 and $5.17 (Table V, pages 46 and 47). Buyout managers earn lower revenue per managed dollar but more per partner, and build on experience by raising larger funds (abstract).

CAUTION

The authors' volatility assumptions are large (90 per cent for each venture investment, 60 per cent for buyout, page 24) and their sample is one large investor's records, so the numbers are not directly transferable to infrastructure. The page uses a single-exit closed form (my simplification) and lets students set their own volatility.

RETURN TO THIS IN THE CASE

The case section on return, risk and exit, and the question of who is paid for what and what changes when a performance fee is waived. The Week 1 page on fee drag asks the same question from the investor's side.

SOURCES

Metrick and Yasuda (2007), Wharton Rodney L. White Center Working Paper 17-07, pages 1 to 3, 10 to 12, 16, 24 and 46 to 47; the published version cited above.

title: The Value of Fixed and Variable Fees
notes:
INTERACTIVE: web/fees-and-carry.html (button at top right)

THE FIGURE

Left panel: the carry the manager is paid at exit as a function of the fund's gross proceeds, for 20 per cent carry with an 8 per cent hurdle and full catch-up, and for 20 per cent with no hurdle, on a commitment of 100 with a 10-year life. With the hurdle, nothing is paid until proceeds reach 100 x 1.08^10, about 216; between that point and about 245 the manager takes all the profit above the hurdle (the catch-up); beyond it the manager holds 20 per cent of total profit. Right panel: the present value of carry per 100 committed as the volatility of the fund's assets rises from 5 to 60 per cent, for three sets of terms, with a 1.5 per cent fee and a 4 per cent risk-free rate. The value rises with volatility, as for any option.

THE DEFAULT RESULT

With 1.5 per cent fees, 20 per cent carry over an 8 per cent hurdle with catch-up, 20 per cent volatility and a 4 per cent risk-free rate, the fees are worth 12.17 per 100 committed and the carry 5.38, so the fixed share of manager revenue is 69 per cent, in the range of the roughly 60 per cent that Metrick and Yasuda report (working paper abstract), and the fund must earn about 1.9 per cent a year over the return on its investable capital for investors to break even. With the performance fee waived the fixed share is 100 per cent.

HOW IT WAS BUILT

The page prices carry as a call option on a single exit with the Black and Scholes formula at the risk-free rate. No hurdle: carry x max(P minus basis, 0). Hurdle H with full catch-up: max(P minus H, 0) minus (1 minus carry) x max(P minus P*, 0), with P* = (H minus carry x basis) / (1 minus carry). Hurdle without catch-up: carry x max(P minus H, 0). Fees are paid on committed capital for the whole life and come out of the commitment. The fund's gross value is set so that limited partners break even in present value, which gives the excess return the fund must earn. This is a simplification of Metrick and Yasuda's multi-investment simulation. The closed form agrees with a Monte Carlo simulation to about 0.02 in present value per 100 and with the JavaScript copy to 14 decimal places on 200 random settings.

PRESETS

A conventional fund; a fund with its performance fee waived (the announced term of a real fund, with an illustrative 1 per cent management fee because the announcement does not give one); and a riskier fund with no hurdle. The published present values from Table V are shown in the notes of the previous slide, with the warning that the models differ.

QUESTIONS FOR THE CLASS

Raise volatility from 20 to 40 per cent and ask what that does to the value of the carry and to the manager's incentives. Set the carry to zero and ask who gains and who loses.

The case section on return, risk and exit, and the question on what a waived performance fee changes for the manager and the investor.

title: Keel and Müller (1995): Assets against Liabilities
notes:
THE PAPER

Keel, A. and Müller, H. H. (1995), Efficient portfolios in the asset liability context, ASTIN Bulletin 25(1), 33 to 48. It builds on Sharpe, W. F. and Tint, L. G. (1990), Liabilities, a new approach, Journal of Portfolio Management 16(2), 5 to 10 (Winter), which I could not retrieve and know only through Keel and Müller's account (pages 33 to 36). The PDF of Keel and Müller is an optical-character scan with garbled symbols, so I checked the equations against the structure of the argument and against the standard algebra.

THE MODEL

The investor has assets A0 and liabilities L0 with funding ratio f0 = A0 / L0, and the liability grows at a random rate (the growth of a pension liability depends on interest rates, inflation and real wages, footnote 1, page 34). The return on the surplus is R_S = R_A(x) minus R_L / f0 (equation 2, page 35), and the investor solves the mean-variance problem of maximising gamma times expected surplus return less half the variance of surplus return, for weights x summing to one (problem (0), pages 35 and 36).

THE RESULT

The efficient portfolios are x* = x_MIN + gamma z*, where x_MIN is the minimum-risk portfolio and z* is a return-generating component that does not depend on the liability; the liability shifts x_MIN by a component that is linear in 1/f0 and does not depend on the investor's risk tolerance, so the efficient set shifts in parallel (equations 6 to 12, pages 38 and 39). If the liability's growth rate depends linearly on several factors, such as the bond return, inflation and economic growth, the liability component decomposes further (section 3). An asset correlated with the liability earns a place in the minimum-risk portfolio whatever its own risk. The authors note that the model applies to many liabilities and to non-traded assets, and that the original Markowitz problem is the special case with a zero liability (pages 34 to 36).

WHY IT FITS INFRASTRUCTURE

The OECD paper gives the investor's case: infrastructure's long duration and inflation linkage can match long liabilities (Della Croce 2012, page 7). The model says that case is a statement about a correlation, which can be tested, and not about the asset's own volatility.

CAUTION

The model is one-period, has no illiquidity and allows short positions in its closed form, so the page adds a long-only search and an illiquidity break-even of my own. Andonov, Kräussl and Rauh (2021) find that closed infrastructure funds carry risk much like other private funds and that their cash flows are procyclical (pages 3882 and 3883), which would weaken the link to the liability.

RETURN TO THIS IN THE CASE

The case section on the pension scheme's reasons for investing, and the question of what return a scheme gives up for the assets it wants and what it must believe about the link to its liability.

title: Three Models of the Fund Compared
notes:
THE TABLE

The synthesis slide of the focus part and, if time is short, the one to keep. Each model answers a different question about the same vehicle, and an investor needs all three answers before it commits.

Takahashi and Alexander (2002) explains when the money moves. It predicts that capital is called early and returned late, so an investor's net position is negative before it is positive and its exposure peaks mid-life. The evidence is the model's wide adoption as the standard planning tool, not a test; Karatas et al. (2021) and Luxenberg et al. (2022) both use it as a benchmark and criticise its determinism. Its limit is that it says nothing about fees, valuation or return.

Metrick and Yasuda (2010) explains who is paid for what. It predicts that carried interest is worth more the riskier the fund and that most manager revenue is fixed, and its test is the authors' own: 238 funds, about 60 per cent fixed (working paper). Its limit is that the data come from one large investor and the value of carry depends on volatility assumptions that are hard to observe.

Keel and Müller (1995), after Sharpe and Tint (1990), explains what the investor needs the asset to do. It predicts that a long-dated asset earns its place by its correlation with the liability and not only by its own risk. The evidence is theoretical in the paper itself, and the test is empirical elsewhere: Andonov, Kräussl and Rauh (2021) find that closed infrastructure funds carry risk like other private funds and procyclical cash flows (pages 3882 to 3883), which would weaken the correlation the model needs. Its limit is that it is one period and ignores illiquidity.

HOW THE THREE FIT

They give an investor three tests of a fund. Can it afford the calls and wait for the distributions, and what must it hold in reserve? Does the manager's pay align with its interest, and what does the fund have to earn to cover it? Does the asset do for the liability what the investor says it does? A fund that passes one only should be questioned.

THE LINK TO THE CASE

Students should arrive at the case able to put each test to a real fund. The case questions use the three tests; the discussion in the second hour is where they are applied.

title: Risk and Return of Unlisted Infrastructure Funds
notes:
THE FIGURE

Left panel: the generalised public market equivalent (GPME) of closed infrastructure funds raised in 2002 to 2018, from Andonov, Kräussl and Rauh (2021), Table 6 (page 3908) and the text (page 3909). The method is Korteweg and Nagel's stochastic discount factor valuation. Against the S&P 500 alone, the GPME is minus 0.067; risk-adjusted for the S&P 500 and Treasury bills, minus 0.257. A GPME of zero corresponds to a public market equivalent of one (page 3908). The authors read minus 0.257 as an abnormal loss of $0.257 per dollar of commitment in present value, comparable to venture capital (introduction); it arises because the SDF parameter b takes the value 6.269, which implies a market beta above one (page 3909). The sample is 145 funds that called at least 25 per cent of commitments (note to Table 6). Right panel: cross-sectional dispersion of the standard PME, 0.31 for infrastructure against 0.28 for real estate, 0.36 for buyout and 0.56 for venture capital (page 3882).

THE POINTS

The authors test, and reject, the hypothesis that closed infrastructure funds deliver more stable and diversifying cash flows than other alternatives (page 3882). Infrastructure funds' average PME is 0.93, below buyout, venture capital and real estate (page 3882; this is the figure Week 1 used, and Week 3 adds the risk adjustment and the dispersion). Only venture capital appears riskier (page 3882). One suggested reason for the high risk is leverage, since infrastructure deals are typically financed with a high proportion of debt: the median transaction is 66 per cent debt and 34 per cent equity, and social infrastructure is highest at a median of 88 per cent, in a subsample of 683 transactions (page 3909, Internet Appendix Table IA.12). Despite weak performance, closed infrastructure fund assets under management rose from $59 billion in 2008 to $486 billion in 2019 (page 3883).

CAUTIONS

The GPME depends on the factor model and the benchmark, and the sample is of funds that report performance, which the paper shows is biased towards funds with quick exits (Table 4; see the next slide). Gupta and van Nieuwerburgh (2021), cited in the authors' introduction, find a smaller risk-adjusted loss of minus six cents per dollar invested. This is evidence about the fund vehicle, not about infrastructure assets held directly.

RETURN TO THIS IN THE CASE

The case's return target should be read against this evidence: a net target of 8 to 10 per cent is close to the average net IRR in the data (the Week 1 slide 'Funds Are Not the Asset'), and the case section on return, risk and exit asks what has to be true for a fund to beat the evidence.

title: Exits, Cash Flows and Investor Type
notes:
THE TABLE

Andonov, Kräussl and Rauh (2021), two sets of regression results. First row: a 10 percentage point increase in the share of deals exited in the first five years is associated with a 0.085 higher PME, a 2.575 percentage point higher net IRR and a 0.079 higher multiple of invested capital (text, page 3883; the regression is in Table 4, printed page 3899). Second row: public investors (public pension funds, sovereign wealth funds and government agencies) receive a 0.026 lower PME, a 1.810 percentage point lower net IRR and a 0.038 lower multiple than private investors (text, page 3884; Table 8, printed page 3915). The deal-level controls include project stage, region and industry, and the underperformance is not driven by home deals (page 3884).

THE POINTS

The closed fund structure gives managers an incentive to exit the best-performing assets quickly, as in other private markets, so performance is strongly related to quick exits (page 3883). Even though infrastructure funds hold tangible assets frequently backed by concession agreements, the incentives of closed funds seem incompatible with investors' expectations of stable, long-lasting income streams (page 3883). The authors also show that net cash flows are high when the price-dividend ratio is high and the yield spread low, in the way of other private funds (page 3883), and that adding infrastructure funds to a portfolio of buyout or venture capital funds gives no detectable cash-flow volatility benefit (page 3883). The investor-type result: public investors increase their exposure to closed funds over time more than private investors, public investors that have signed the UN Principles for Responsible Investment make 0.759 more infrastructure investments a year than those that have not, and adoption of the principles and shocks to voluntary ESG regulation explain around 25 to 40 per cent of the higher number of investments by public investors (abstract). The authors suggest that the underperformance of public investors is at least partly driven by stronger social externalities and politicised governance, and that if the expected real return is about 5 per cent, the lower IRR amounts to about 30 per cent of it (abstract and page 3884; the paper's own calculation).

LINK TO THE MODELS

The exit incentive is the second model at work: carry is an option on proceeds, and an option holder who exits when in the money has a reason to sell winners early. The procyclical cash flows are the first model's call and distribution rates responding to market conditions, which the deterministic model does not allow. The investor-type result bears on the third model, because an investor that accepts a lower return for social externalities has a different objective from the surplus-risk minimiser.

notes:
THE FIGURE

Moody's Investors Service (2020), Default and recovery rates for project finance bank loans, 1983 to 2018: sustainable project finance bank loans, 17 August 2020, Exhibit 2 (page 8). Ten-year cumulative default rate for the total data sample (7,354 projects): 5.0 per cent on the Basel definition and 3.2 per cent on Moody's; green use-of-proceeds 4.9 and 2.9; non-green 7.1 and 4.7; social (hospitals and schools) 1.1 and 0.4. Average ultimate recovery for the total sample is 81.5 per cent (Basel) and 79.5 per cent (Moody's), with a median of 100 per cent, and about 9.3 per cent of observations recover only 0 to 24 per cent (pages 6 and 7). The study covers three sectors (infrastructure, power, oil and gas), 85.7 per cent of the 8,583 project finance bank loans in the full data set (pages 2 and 6). The March 2020 study of the whole data set reports a 10-year cumulative default rate of 5.5 per cent (Basel) and 3.7 per cent (Moody's) and average recovery of 77.9 and 75.8 per cent (page 6); I did not retrieve it.

THE POINTS

Project finance debt behaves differently from the equity evidence on the last slides: it has a long public record, defaults are rare and recoveries are high. The Basel definition captures a wider range of defaults than Moody's (page 2). The report's own interpretation is that sustainability is not the principal driver of the lower default rates of green and social projects; contractual arrangements, the phase of the credit cycle, jurisdiction, industry and project-specific risks are, and the social projects have a high prevalence of availability-based payments from governmental offtakers (page 1). None of the defaults on social projects or green power projects was caused by market risk, which reflects availability payments and power purchase agreements (page 7).

CAUTIONS

This is an addendum on sustainable project finance, so the headline figures are for the total sample of the three sectors and not for the whole of project finance. The social sample in emerging markets is tiny (32 projects in EMDE-A and 14 in EMDE-B, of which 2 defaulted, page 6), so the emerging-market social figure is not robust. The data come from a consortium of banks and are not public. The study measures bank loans and not bonds.

HOW IT FITS THE WEEK

The week's earlier evidence is about equity in funds, which is thin and discouraging. The debt evidence is the opposite, and it explains why infrastructure debt funds have grown (old deck slides 34 and 35). A fund that issues debt against contracted revenue is the structure in the data centre financing on slide 7.

CAUSES OF DEFAULT

In the EEA and EEA/OECD the most prevalent cause of default is market risk (31.8 and 37.5 per cent), with country risk the primary cause of fewer than 5 per cent of defaults. In the emerging-market subsets country risk is the most prevalent cause (35.7 per cent in EMDE-A and 45.5 in EMDE-B), followed by construction risk and market risk (page 7). Defaults often cluster around country risk and industry events (page 1).

WHY IT MATTERS FOR A FUND

The risk of the debt depends on when the investor enters. A lender or fund that buys at financial close bears the high-risk years and one that buys a seasoned operating loan bears the low-risk years and pays a lower yield for it. That is the difference between the value-add and core-plus strategies that fund managers describe, and it is why the J-curve of a value-add fund (slide 10) is deeper than that of an income fund.

notes:
THE FIGURE

Attridge, S. and Engen, L. (2019), Blended finance in the poorest countries: the need for a better approach, Overseas Development Institute, April 2019. Private finance mobilised per $1 of MDB and DFI commitment, 2013 to 2015, for nine selected institutions: $0.75 overall, $0.37 in low-income countries (LICs), $1.06 in lower-middle-income countries (LMICs) and $0.65 in upper-middle-income countries (UMICs) (key findings, page 11; Figures 3 and 4 and text, pages 37 and 38). The overall figure comes from $64.2 billion of commitments that mobilised $47.9 billion of private finance (page 37), a ratio of 0.75. Leverage ratios are lowest in infrastructure in both LICs and middle-income countries, and sector leverage in middle-income countries is at least double that in LICs across the board (page 38). Page numbers are the printed pages, which equal the PDF pages.

THE ARGUMENT

The report's headline is that expectations of blended finance are unrealistic: 'billions to billions' is more plausible than 'billions to trillions' (key findings, page 11). With an SDG financing gap of $2.5 trillion a year in developing countries (UNCTAD 2014, cited on page 10), the premise of the push is that public money can mobilise several times its value. ODI's estimate is that it mobilises less than its own value, and much less in the poorest countries. The authors say the exercise is illustrative and the data limited, because institutions publish little project-level data (page 37), so the figures are indicative, and they call for better data (Recommendation 3, page 13).

WHERE IT CONNECTS

Week 2 (the slide 'Mobilisation Effects of Multilateral Lenders') used Broccolini et al. (2019) for the opposite finding, that multilateral lending mobilises private lenders, with large effects relative to a low average. The two are not contradictory. Broccolini et al. measure the effect of an MDB's presence on syndicated bank lending in country-sector-years, and ODI measures the ratio of private finance to the public commitment in blended deals. The difference between them is a useful exercise for students.

CAUTIONS

The ratio measures what institutions report as mobilised, with definitions that differ across institutions, and the sample is of nine institutions. The report is a policy paper by a think tank.

RETURN TO THIS IN THE CASE

The case is a domestic one, and this slide is the contrast: private capital follows a mobilisation ratio abroad, and at home a public scheme can act as an anchor investor. Ask what an anchor investor changes about the terms.

SOURCE

Attridge and Engen (2019), pages 3, 10, 11, 13, 37 and 38.

title: Private Finance Follows Credit Ratings
notes:
THE FIGURES

Right panel: Attridge and Engen (2019) estimate that 96.3 per cent of the private finance mobilised through blended finance between 2012 and 2015 flowed to countries with a credit rating, which most LICs do not have (the 3.7 per cent shown for unrated countries is the remainder, my arithmetic) (key findings, page 11; text, page 53). Left panel: Moody's (2020), page 7, shows the share of project finance defaults for which country risk was the primary cause, under 5 per cent in the European Economic Area and EEA/OECD subsets, 35.7 per cent in EMDE-A and 45.5 per cent in EMDE-B. The left bar is drawn at 5 and labelled 'under 5', because Moody's gives only the bound.

THE ARGUMENT

Both sources read the same barrier from different sides. ODI's reading from the investor's side: private commercial finance will not flow freely to countries where the investment climate is challenging, markets are not functioning and the risk-adjusted return is uncompetitive; blended finance may tip the balance but will not work if the economic fundamentals are not in place (page 11). The lender's side: where a project is in a country with weak institutions, country risk becomes the most common cause of default (Moody's, page 7). The old Week 3 deck (slides 47 to 53) names five barriers, currency, pipeline, ticket size, local capital markets and ratings; I have not verified that list against a source, and the two exhibits here support only the ratings and country-risk barriers.

THE PRIORITY POINT

Helen asked for prioritisation, and the point to keep from this part is narrow. Capital goes where contracts can be enforced and risks can be priced, and instruments cannot supply what the investment climate does not. That connects back to the week's evidence on funds and debt.

CAUTIONS

The 96.3 per cent is a share of mobilised private finance in a four-year sample of nine institutions and not a share of all private investment; the source warns that mobilisation data are limited (page 37). Moody's causes of default are shares of defaults in a sample, not default rates, and EMDE social projects are few (page 6).

RETURN TO THIS IN THE CASE

The case is in a market with a credit rating and a legal system investors know, which is exactly the setting the evidence says capital looks for. The question is what that does to the terms.

SOURCES

Attridge and Engen (2019), pages 11, 37 and 53; Moody's (2020), pages 6 and 7.

title: Megginson and Netter: The Survey Evidence
notes:
THE PAPER

Megginson, W. L. and Netter, J. M. (2001), From state to market: a survey of empirical studies on privatization, Journal of Economic Literature 39(2), 321 to 389. I read the December 1998 conference draft (FEEM and the SBF Bourse de Paris and New York Stock Exchange conference, working paper NDL 1999-001), because the published article was not retrievable; the printed page of the draft is the PDF page minus two, and the published version is longer and differs in detail. The draft's abstract says the debate over the relative performance of state-owned and private firms has largely been resolved in favour of private ownership.

THE EVIDENCE

Privatisation had reduced state-owned enterprises sharply in some places, particularly Western Europe, but outside the European Union they retain much of their historic role (page 2). Of the 1,000 largest companies in a 1998 ranking, 75 were privatised firms, and governments have raised more than $500 billion through some 630 public share offerings since 1977 (page 9). The authors survey studies that compare performance before and after divestiture. One of the multi-country studies they summarise, by Galal, Jones, Tandon and Vogelsang (1992), compares the post-privatisation performance of 12 large firms, mostly airlines and regulated utilities, in Britain, Chile, Malaysia and Mexico with a counterfactual of staying state-owned; it finds net welfare gains in 11 of the 12 cases, equal on average to 26 per cent of the firms' pre-divestiture sales (the summary table in the appendix, printed page 64). The authors conclude that the evidence supports private ownership and that privatisation significantly improves operating and financial performance (abstract).

THE QUALIFICATION

The survey reports the Hart, Shleifer and Vishny result: public ownership is preferred only when cost reduction opportunities lead to significant non-contractible quality reductions, innovation is relatively unimportant, competition is weak and consumer choice ineffective, and reputational mechanisms are weak, (pages 12 to 13). It is the same logic as Hart (2003) in the Week 2 deck, and it is the reason the Week 2 slide on bundling asks what the contract can specify. The survey also notes that the British electricity and utility privatisations were accompanied by regulation and that Beesley and Littlechild found the RPI-X price regulation adopted in the UK much superior to US rate-of-return regulation (page 18).

CAUTIONS

The survey is of a literature that is dominated by studies of large firms with good data and of privatisations that were chosen by governments, which makes selection a concern. A conference draft from 1998 is not the published survey. The next slide sets the survey against a later study of local services that finds no cost advantage.

RETURN TO THIS IN THE CASE

The case is a public body choosing a private partner for a local social purpose. The question is when the Hart, Shleifer and Vishny conditions favouring public provision apply and when they do not.

SOURCE

Megginson and Netter, From state to market, December 1998 draft (FEEM NDL 1999-001), pages 2, 8, 9, 12 to 13, 18, 21 and the appendix summary table (printed page 64); the published article is Journal of Economic Literature 39(2), 321 to 389, not retrieved.

title: Two Readings of Private Provision
notes:
THE TABLE

The two sources set side by side. Megginson and Netter survey the privatisation of state-owned enterprises, mostly large firms and often in competitive or liberalising markets, using before-and-after and matched comparisons, and conclude that private ownership outperforms. Bel, Fageda and Warner (2010), Is private production of public services cheaper than public production? A meta-regression analysis of solid waste and water services, Journal of Policy Analysis and Management 29(3), 553 to 577, which I read in the IREA working paper 2009/23 (33 pages; the journal reference is from a search record and unverified), analyse local services. They conduct a meta-regression analysis of 27 econometric studies that compare costs of private and public production (introduction, page 2), from 38 published papers and working papers identified (page 2), and find no systematic support for lower costs with private production (abstract, page 1).

HOW THE TWO CAN BOTH BE RIGHT

The differences between study results are explained by the period of the analysis, service characteristics and the policy environment (abstract). They find some evidence of publication bias, meaning that papers finding significant cost savings are more likely to be published (page 23), and that cost differences are less likely in more recent studies, and more likely in solid waste collection than in water distribution, given the lack of competition and higher asset specificity of the latter (page 23). Water distribution is a service of high asset specificity that tends towards natural monopoly, with few expectations of competition (page 3), so the privatisation of a network is the case where the survey's assumption of competition is weakest. The authors' conclusion is that to ensure cost savings, more attention should go to the cost characteristics of the service, the transaction costs involved and the policy environment stimulating competition, and less to the debate over public versus private delivery (abstract). They note that in neither service is competition expected to persist over time (page 3).

THE LINK TO THE WEEK

The week has argued that the vehicle matters more than the label of the asset. The ownership debate is the same point at the level of the country: a private partner is a means, and its value depends on contract design and competition, which are the subjects of Week 2 and of the case.

CAUTIONS

A meta-regression is limited to the available studies, which cover two local services and mostly cross-sectional comparisons (page 15 and following); it cannot speak to the large infrastructure assets in this deck. The Megginson and Netter figures are from a 1998 draft.

RETURN TO THIS IN THE CASE

The case asks a local public body to partner with a private manager. The question is what the evidence from both readings suggests it should specify and monitor.

SOURCES

Bel, G., Fageda, X. and Warner, M. E. (2009), Is private production of public services cheaper than public production? IREA Working Papers 2009/23 (printed page equals PDF page), pages 1 to 3, 15, 16 and 23; Megginson and Netter (draft of December 1998) as on the previous slide.

title: Case Study: Newcore Capital and the Swansea Social Infrastructure Partnership (Hugo Llewelyn, Newcore Capital)
notes:
AN OUTLINE ONLY

By design this is one slide naming the ground the case covers and leaving the discussion to the guest, Hugo Llewelyn, Chief Executive Officer of Newcore Capital. It states no facts about the case, takes no position and makes no claim, so it cannot spoil what he says. The title follows the records' spelling of the surname and the company (the Newcore Capital announcement, the speaker note and Helen's instruction agree).

THE FIVE HEADINGS

The fund and its partners; the investor's problem; terms, returns and risks; measuring outcomes; and discussion with the guest. They follow the structure of the case (the fund and the investor, the terms, the strategy and the measure of outcomes) without saying anything about any of them.

HOW THE WEEK PREPARES THE CASE

The first hour is deliberately broader than the case. It tells students who invests and why (slides 3 to 5), shows how capital reaches a project through a vehicle (6 and 7), and gives three models of a fund (8 to 15) and the evidence on funds, debt, emerging markets and ownership (16 to 23). Students should leave with three tests they can put to any fund: can the investor afford the calls and wait for the distributions, is the manager's pay aligned with its own, and does the asset do for the liability what the investor says it does. The second hour is where they apply the tests to one real fund.

WHAT IS STILL OPEN

The format of the session (guest lecture or case contribution), the date and the decision the case turns on are open, and the case template for Hugo is drafted separately. The title of the case is a working title. A discrepancy to note: the Newcore announcement's headline says Swansea Council is the limited partner, while its text says the investor is the City and County of Swansea Pension Fund, with the council as its administering authority. The case uses the text's wording.

DECLARATION

Andrew Baum, a member of the Global Infrastructure Advisory Panel, has signed communications as Chairman of Newcore Capital and helps build the case with Helen, so the link should be declared in the case, the session and any publication.
